bookTitle: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
generalAssumptions: Zero counterparty default risk in exchange-cleared trades backed by central clearing houses.
Bilateral OTC forwards carry direct counterparty credit exposure unless cleared via a Central Counterparty (CCP).
Continuous price quotation during exchange and interbank trading hours.
Ignoring transaction costs, commissions, and bid-ask spreads unless explicitly specified in numerical examples.

facts.statement: A futures contract is a standardized legal agreement between two parties to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified future date for a predetermined price, traded on organized exchanges such as CME Group, ICE, Euronext, and Eurex.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: A futures contract is an agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a certain time in the future for a certain price. Unlike forward contracts, futures contracts are normally traded on an exchange.

facts.statement: A forward contract is an over-the-counter (OTC) derivative agreement between two private financial institutions or corporations to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified future date for a negotiated price, non-standardized and subject to counterparty credit risk.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: A forward contract is particularly simple. It is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a certain future time for a certain price. It is traded in the over-the-counter market.

facts.statement: In any forward or futures contract, the party that agrees to buy the underlying asset assumes the long position, whereas the party that agrees to sell the underlying asset assumes the short position.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: The party that agrees to buy has what is termed a long position; the party that agrees to sell has what is termed a short position.

facts.statement: The spot price is the quoted price for immediate or near-immediate delivery of an asset, whereas the forward/futures price is agreed upon today for delivery and settlement at a specified future date.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: In contrast to a spot contract, which is an agreement to buy or sell an asset today, a forward contract fixes the delivery price today for settlement at a later date.

facts.statement: The Over-the-Counter (OTC) market is a decentralized interbank network where financial institutions, fund managers, and multinational corporations trade customized derivatives directly with one another, typically featuring larger average contract notionals than exchange-traded derivatives.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: The OTC market is a telephone and computer-linked network of dealers who do not occupy a physical trading floor. Trades are usually between two financial institutions or between a financial institution and one of its corporate clients.

facts.statement: Derivatives trading has evolved from the traditional open-outcry system—where floor traders physically shouted bids and offers using hand signals in exchange pits—to electronic matching engines that enable algorithmic and high-frequency trading across global exchanges.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Traditionally, futures contracts were traded using the open-outcry system... In recent years, electronic trading systems have largely replaced open outcry.

facts.statement: Foreign exchange market makers quote exchange rates with a two-way price: the bid rate at which the bank buys foreign currency and the offer (ask) rate at which the bank sells foreign currency. On May 13, 2015, quotes for USD/GBP were Spot 1.5746/1.5750, 1-Month Forward 1.5742/1.5747, and 3-Month Forward 1.5736/1.5742.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Quotes for the exchange rate between the British pound and the U.S. dollar on May 13, 2015: Spot Bid 1.5746 / Offer 1.5750; 3-Month Forward Bid 1.5736 / Offer 1.5742.

numericalDetails.context: Bank FX foreign exchange market quotes on May 13, 2015 for spot and forward contracts

facts.statement: In Hull Example 1.1, ImportCo must pay £10,000,000 in 3 months for British imports. To eliminate currency appreciation risk, ImportCo buys £10,000,000 in the 3-month forward market at the bank's offer price of 1.5742 USD/GBP, locking in an exact cash outlay of $15,742,000.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Suppose that on May 13, 2015, the treasurer of a corporation knows that the corporation will pay 10 million pounds in three months... The corporation can buy 10 million pounds in the three-month forward market at 1.5742. This locks in the payment at $15,742,000.

facts.statement: At maturity T, the gross terminal payoff for a long forward contract with delivery price K and spot price S_T is S_T - K. Conversely, the gross terminal payoff for a short forward contract is K - S_T. Unlike options, forward contracts have zero upfront cost or premium.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: The payoff from a long position in a forward contract on one unit of an asset is S_T - K, where K is the delivery price and S_T is the spot price of the asset at maturity. Similarly, the payoff from a short position is K - S_T.

payoffVsProfit.formulaProfit: Profit = Payoff - 0 = S_T - K (Zero upfront premium for forward contracts)
payoffVsProfit.explanation: Because a forward contract costs zero to enter initially (zero premium), the terminal payoff is identical to net economic profit before financing costs.

facts.topic: Agricultural Origins of Futures at CBOT
facts.statement: Futures markets originated in 1848 with the founding of the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) to standardize grain quality and quantity (e.g. 5,000 bushels per contract), resolving the dilemma between farmers (facing catastrophic harvest price collapse during September bumper crops) and grain merchants (facing devastating price spikes during crop failures).

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) was established in 1848 to bring farmers and merchants together. Initially, its main task was to standardize the quantities and qualities of the grains that were traded. Standard grain contracts were established at 5,000 bushels.

numericalDetails.context: CBOT standardization of agricultural grain contracts to mitigate harvest price risk

facts.statement: In Business Snapshot 1.1, Lehman Brothers collapsed on September 15, 2008 in the largest bankruptcy filing in U.S. history. Unregulated by commercial bank capital adequacy rules, Lehman operated at an extreme leverage ratio of 31:1 in 2007, meaning a minimal asset decline of just 3% to 4% was sufficient to completely wipe out all corporate equity capital.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy protection. It was the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history... In 2007, its leverage ratio was 31:1. This means that only a 3% to 4% decline in the value of its assets was needed to wipe out its equity.

numericalDetails.context: Lehman Brothers 31:1 leverage ratio before bankruptcy where a 3-4% asset loss wiped out all equity

facts.topic: Lehman OTC Counterparty Web and Rehypothecation
facts.statement: At its failure, Lehman Brothers held more than 1,000,000 outstanding OTC derivative contracts across approximately 8,000 counterparties. Because client collateral posted with Lehman had been re-hypothecated (reused to finance Lehman's proprietary positions), counterparties suffered severe delays and legal entanglement lasting years.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Lehman was an active participant in the OTC derivatives market with over one million outstanding contracts involving about 8,000 counterparties. The bankruptcy led to huge legal costs and protracted disputes over collateral rehypothecation.

numericalDetails.context: Lehman Brothers OTC derivatives exposure at time of default

facts.statement: Systemic risk is the risk that a default by a single major financial institution will trigger a cascading ripple effect of counterparty defaults across the interconnected financial network (Bank A defaults -> Bank B suffers severe losses and defaults -> Bank C collapses), threatening the integrity of the entire global financial system.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Systemic risk is the risk that the failure of one financial institution will lead to a cascading failure of other financial institutions... The failure of Bank A causes large losses for Bank B, which in turn causes Bank B to fail, impacting Bank C.

facts.topic: Post-2008 Central Clearing and SEF Regulations
facts.statement: To prevent systemic cascades, post-2008 international regulations mandated three core structural reforms for OTC derivatives: mandatory trading on Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs), mandatory clearing through Central Counterparties (CCPs) that novate trades to become buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, and mandatory recording in Trade Repositories.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Post-crisis regulations introduced three major changes: 1. Standardized OTC derivatives must be traded on Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs). 2. Standardized OTC derivatives must be cleared through Central Counterparties (CCPs). 3. All trades must be reported to Trade Repositories.

facts.topic: Size Comparison: OTC vs Exchange-Traded Derivatives
facts.statement: As of December 2014, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) estimated total notional principal outstanding in the OTC derivatives market at approximately $630 trillion, compared to $65 trillion for exchange-traded derivatives, while the gross market value of OTC contracts was approximately $21 trillion.

sourceCitation.book: Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets (John C. Hull)
sourceCitation.excerpt: In December 2014, the total notional principal for OTC derivatives was estimated at $630 trillion, compared to $65 trillion for exchange-traded contracts. The gross market value was about $21 trillion.

numericalDetails.context: BIS December 2014 global derivatives market size survey
